newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle ends shortened mission.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle ends shortened mission.

text.p: The space shuttle Columbia ended a science mission curtailed by a malfunctioning power generator with a smooth landing on Tuesday at NASA's Florida spaceport.

But as the orbiter sat on its Cape Canaveral runway, space agency officials were considering sending it up again soon to accomplish the aborted mission's objectives, with a launch possible as early as July 2, sources at the space agency said.
The $2 billion gliding spaceship soared through wispy clouds and touched down at the Kennedy Space Centre at 2:33 p.m. EDT (1833 GMT), less than four days after blasting off.
"Columbia welcome home. Your landing and deorbit looked great," mission control's Dominic Gorie said.
NASA ordered an early end to the planned 16-day science mission because one of the shuttle's three electricity-generating fuel cells was behaving unusually and could have sparked a fire or explosion.
The loss of the device did not affect the landing of the $2 billion spaceplane, which can fly safely powered by two working generators.

"Most of our equipment will be running that we require for landing," pilot Susan Still had told a news conference before firing Columbia's twin braking rockets at 1:31 p.m. (1731 GMT) as they orbited high above the Indian Ocean.
Some landing systems were activated later than usual to conserve power, she explained.

It was only the third time in 83 missions since the shuttle programme began in 1981 that NASA called a shuttle home early because of a mechanical breakdown. A faulty fuel cell was to blame for cutting short NASA's second shuttle flight in November 1981 and a failed navigation device ended a 1991 mission prematurely.
There were signs of trouble with the $5 million fuel cell during Columbia's countdown, but it appeared to have returned to normal before Friday's blastoff.
Engineers had seen similar pre-launch readings from other generators which did not develop problems in flight.
One such fuel cell on shuttle Atlantis was being replaced on Tuesday as precaution, NASA spokesman Bruce Buckingham said. Atlantis is scheduled to fly to the Russian space station Mir next month.
Columbia's astronauts left orbit with only a fraction of their $84 million research programme accomplished.
"We're just sorry we're having to close up shop early," mission control's Marc Garneau told the crew as they shutdown Columbia's laboratory early on Tuesday.

Columbia's crew of seven had been living in near-darkness since the troublesome power generator was shut down on Sunday, working with flashlights. All non-essential equipment including most of the lighting was turned off to conserve power for scientific experiments in the shuttle's laboratory.

Scientists have requested a rerun of the mission, which was to have studied the behaviour of fire in space, the growth of plants, the structure of proteins and the manufacture of ultra-pure materials.
